Equation (7.2) was derived in 1921 by Kármán [7], who wrote it in the

convenient form of the _momentum thickness_ _θ_ :

Momentum thickness is thus a measure of total plate drag. Kármán then
noted that the drag also equals the integrated wall shear stress along the plate:

Meanwhile, the derivative of Eq. (7.3), with _U_ = constant, is

By comparing this with Eq. (7.4) Kármán arrived at what is now called the
_momentum integral relation_ for flat-plate boundary layer flow:

It is valid for either laminar or turbulent flat-plate flow.

To get a numerical result for laminar flow, Kármán assumed that the
velocity profiles had an approximately parabolic shape

which makes it possible to estimate both momentum thickness and wall
shear:

By substituting (7.7) into (7.5) and rearranging we obtain

where _ν_ = _μ_ / _ρ_ . We can integrate from 0 to _x_, assuming that _δ_ = 0 at _x_ = 0, the
leading edge:

This is the desired thickness estimate. It is all approximate, of course, part
of Kármán’s _momentum integral theory_ [7], but it is startlingly accurate, being
only 10 percent higher than the known accepted solution for laminar flat-plate
flow, which we gave as Eq. (7.1a).

By combining Eqs. (7.9) and (7.7) we also obtain a shear stress estimate
along the plate:

Again this estimate, in spite of the crudeness of the profile assumption [Eq.
(7.6)] is only 10 percent higher than the known exact laminar-plate-flow solution

, treated in Sec. 7.4. The dimensionless quantity _cf_, called the _skin_
_friction coefficient,_ is analogous to the friction factor _f_ in ducts.

A boundary layer can be judged as “thin” if, say, the ratio _δ_ / _x_ is less than
about 0.1. This occurs at or at Re _x_ = 2500. For Re _x_ less than
2500 we can estimate that boundary layer theory fails because the thick layer has
a significant effect on the outer inviscid flow. The upper limit on Re _x_ for laminar
flow is about 3 × 10 <sup>6</sup>, where measurements on a smooth flat plate [8] show that
the flow undergoes transition to a turbulent boundary layer. From 3 × 10 <sup>6</sup>

upward the turbulent Reynolds number may be arbitrarily large, and a practical
limit at present is 5 × 10 <sup>10</sup> for oil supertankers.

**Fig. 7.4 Displacement effect of a boundary layer.**

Another interesting effect of a boundary layer is its small but finite
displacement of the outer streamlines. As shown in Fig. 7.4, outer streamlines
must deflect outward a distance _δ_ <sup>*</sup> ( _x_ ) to satisfy conservation of mass between the
inlet and outlet:

The quantity _δ_ <sup>*</sup> is called the _displacement thickness_ of the boundary layer. To
relate it to _u_ ( _y_ ), cancel _ρ_ and _b_ from Eq. (7.11), evaluate the left integral, and
slyly add and subtract _U_ from the right integrand:

Thus the ratio of _δ_ <sup>*</sup> / _δ_ varies only with the dimensionless velocity profile
shape _u_ / _U_ .

Introducing our profile approximation (7.6) into (7.12), we obtain by
integration this approximate result:

These estimates are only 6 percent away from the exact solutions for laminar
flat-plate flow given in Sec. 7.4: Since _δ_ <sup>*</sup> is much
smaller than _x_ for large Re _x_ and the outer streamline slope _V_ / _U_ is proportional to

_δ_ <sup>*</sup>, we conclude that the velocity normal to the wall is much smaller than the
velocity parallel to the wall. This is a key assumption in boundary layer theory
(Sec. 7.3).

We also conclude from the success of these simple parabolic estimates that
Kármán’s momentum integral theory is effective and useful. Many details of this
theory are given in Refs. 1 to 3.
